faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Primostar 1 used for?
faqs.answer: It is an upright transmitted light microscope for education and teaching, built for brightfield viewing of stained specimens in biology, medicine, and life science practicals.

faqs.question: Does it need to be set up before use?

faqs.question: What kind of specimens can I view with it?
faqs.answer: Stained specimens on glass slides with coverslips, both fixed samples and freshly prepared native samples.

faqs.question: Can I use it for whole specimens like insects or plant parts?
faqs.answer: No, that requires a stereo microscope such as the Zeiss Stemi 305, which uses a different optical path for whole, unprepared objects.

faqs.question: What kind of illumination does it use?

faqs.question: Is this suitable for first-time microscope users?

sections.title: Fixed-Köhler Illumination
sections.tabSummary: Why removing an adjustment step matters in a classroom
body: The one adjustment step most classrooms can't afford to lose time on.

Köhler illumination is the standard for even, glare-free microscope lighting, and getting it right normally takes a trained hand: aligning the condenser, centering the field diaphragm, adjusting for each new sample. In a research lab, that is a five-minute task for someone who does it daily. In a classroom of thirty students on their first day with a microscope, it is thirty separate failure points before anyone has actually looked at a cell.

Primostar 1 removes the step entirely. The illumination arrives pre-fixed, so image quality does not depend on whether the last student to use the microscope set it up correctly. A teacher hands the microscope over already working.

rows: Consistent image quality regardless of who used it last

paragraphs: A microscope that tries to handle everything usually handles nothing especially well. Primostar 1 is direct about its scope: stained specimens on glass slides with coverslips, fixed or freshly prepared native samples, viewed by transmitted light in brightfield.

That focus is deliberate, not a limitation. Whole, unprepared specimens, beetles, plant parts, stones, need reflected light and a completely different optical path. Zeiss's own guidance points to a stereo microscope like the Stemi 305 for that work instead. Buying the right tool for each task beats buying one tool that compromises on both.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axioscope 5 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an upright microscope built for biomedical routine and research work, supporting histology, cytology, hematology, and multichannel fluorescence documentation including immunofluorescence and FISH.

faqs.question: How does the four-channel fluorescence feature work?
faqs.answer: Paired with Colibri 3 LED illumination and the Axiocam 203 mono camera, select the channels for UV, blue, green, and red excitation, then press Snap. The system automatically adjusts exposure, acquires each channel, switches wavelengths, and delivers a single overlaid image with a scale bar, without needing a PC.

faqs.question: Does brightfield documentation work the same way?
faqs.answer: Yes, focus the sample and press Snap. The captured color matches exactly what's seen through the eyepieces, with brightness and white balance adjusted automatically.

faqs.question: Is the focus motorized?
faqs.answer: No, Axioscope 5 uses manual Z focus. Motorized focus is a feature of Axioscope 7.

faqs.question: Can Axioscope 5 perform whole slide imaging?
faqs.answer: No, whole slide imaging requires Axioscope 7's motorized stage and Z-control. Axioscope 5 is built for field-of-view documentation and multichannel fluorescence rather than full slide digitization.

faqs.question: What makes Axioscope 7 different from Axioscope 5?
faqs.answer: Axioscope 7 adds a motorized stage and motorized Z-control (autofocus) for scanning and stitching entire slides into whole slide images, with ZEN software supporting full GxP compliance for regulated environments. Axioscope 5 keeps focus manual and is built for routine field-of-view documentation.

faqs.question: Is Axioscope 7 suitable for clinical diagnostics?
faqs.answer: Axioscope 7 is positioned for clinical research labs and biomedical research applications, with ZEN core software supporting GxP compliance where regulated diagnostic workflows require it.

faqs.question: What is the advantage of whole slide imaging on a motorized upright microscope?
faqs.answer: It allows an entire specimen to be digitized automatically, large tissue sections scanned with a motorized stage, focus maintained across the whole sample, and multi-position, multi-channel datasets stitched into a single high-resolution image, useful for archival, remote review, and downstream digital analysis.

faqs.question: Which Axioscope is right for my lab?
faqs.answer: If the work is routine and research documentation, including multichannel fluorescence, without needing to digitize entire slides, Axioscope 5 fits. If the lab needs to scan and archive complete specimens, particularly under regulated conditions, Axioscope 7 is the better fit.

faqs.question: What illumination does it use?
faqs.answer: 10W LED or 50W Halogen for transmitted light, and Colibri 3, Viluma 5/7, or HXP for fluorescence.

faqs.question: Can samples be tracked by barcode?
faqs.answer: Yes, either through a barcode reader connected to the Axiocam 212 color camera, or by scanning with an iPad's camera through Labscope.

faqs.question: Is a shared, two-person view available?

sections.tabSummary: How Colibri 3 and Smart Microscopy handle multichannel fluorescence
body: What used to take four separate manual captures now takes one.

Multichannel fluorescence imaging is normally a stop-start process: select a channel, adjust exposure, capture, switch, adjust again, capture again, then combine everything into an overlay afterward, usually on a connected computer. That's four separate manual decisions before a single usable image exists.

Axioscope 5 removes the stopping. Paired with Colibri 3 and the Axiocam 203 mono camera, select the channels needed for UV, blue, green, and red excitation, then press Snap. The system adjusts exposure time automatically, acquires the image, switches to the next channel, and repeats, on its own. What comes out the other end is a single overlaid multichannel fluorescence image, scale bar included, without needing a PC connected at all.

faqs.question: What is the Zeiss Axio Imager 2 used for?
faqs.answer: It's an upright research microscope platform for high-resolution cellular imaging, used across cell biology, histological examination, and cancer research.

faqs.question: What does the z-drive step size actually mean for the research?
faqs.answer: A 10 nm step size gives precise, repeatable focusing, keeping the sample position stable across a session, which matters directly for reproducible high-resolution imaging.

faqs.question: What stands are available?
faqs.answer: Four: Axio Imager.A2 for manual observation, .D2 for fast switching between observation and imaging, .M2 for highly motorized automated acquisition, and .Z2 for the platform's full motorized capability.

faqs.question: Does it need a connected computer to operate?
faqs.answer: No. With a smart Axiocam camera, images display directly to an external monitor or TV and save straight to a memory stick.

faqs.question: Can it be expanded for optical sectioning?
faqs.answer: Yes, with Apotome 3, giving structured illumination optical sections down to 180 nm resolution.

faqs.question: Can it be used for confocal imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes, the platform is compatible with LSM confocal systems for laser-based imaging and deeper optical sectioning.

faqs.question: Can it support live-cell imaging?
faqs.answer: Yes, with an XL incubator, for imaging live specimens at elevated, controlled temperature.

faqs.question: How many filter sets does it support?
faqs.answer: Up to 10, paired with the ZEISS Viluma multi-LED light source family for spectral flexibility.

faqs.question: What is ZEISS Microscopy Copilot?
faqs.answer: An AI assistant aware of the specific microscope configuration and available ZEN Toolkits, answering questions about experiment setup, automation, and post-processing in natural conversation.

faqs.question: Is this suitable for high-throughput tissue analysis?
faqs.answer: Yes, it's demonstrated directly on high-throughput tissue microarray (TMA) analysis, screening multiple tissue samples across several markers for tumor-immune interaction studies.

faqs.question: How is Axio Imager 2 different from Axioscope 5 or Axioscope 7?
faqs.answer: Axio Imager 2 is built for deeper research applications, offering 10 nm focus precision, four stand options, confocal and optical sectioning expansion, and live-cell imaging support. Axioscope 5 and 7 are positioned for clinical and biomedical routine work and whole slide digitization rather than the same depth of research-grade modularity.

faqs.question: Which cameras is it compatible with?
faqs.answer: The full ZEISS Axiocam portfolio, as well as cameras from other manufacturers.

longForm.heroLead: Cellular structures don't reveal themselves at low resolution, and research doesn't wait for a microscope that's almost precise enough. Axio Imager 2 is built for the detail that cancer research, histology, and cell biology actually demand. The z-drive moves in 10 nm steps, holding focus precisely and keeping it there. A vibration-free imaging cell keeps the filter cubes, camera, and objective in stable proximity, so image quality stays reproducible run after run. A 25 mm field of view means more cells captured per shot, or larger areas scanned faster, without sacrificing resolution to get there. It comes as four distinct stands, A2, D2, M2, and Z2, each built for a different level of automation, from purely manual observation through to full motorized control for laser-based and cryogenic microscopy. Every stand accepts the same modular expansion: Apotome 3 for optical sectioning, an LSM confocal for laser scanning, an XL incubator for live imaging at elevated temperature, and up to 10 filter sets for spectral flexibility. What it captures: cellular detail at research-grade resolution, reproducibly. What it adapts to: the exact level of motorization the work actually requires. body: Choosing the level of automation the research actually needs.

Buying more motorization than a study requires wastes budget. Buying too little means a manual workflow slows down exactly the kind of high-throughput screening or 3D reconstruction work that justifies the platform in the first place. Axio Imager 2 solves that by offering four stands instead of one, each built for a specific point on the automation spectrum.

Axio Imager.A2 is a manual stand, ideal for observation tasks, built with research-grade optics for the finest detail and most accurate color. Axio Imager.D2 suits labs that move constantly between observation and imaging, with an optional motorized reflector turret for automated multi-channel fluorescence. Axio Imager.M2 is highly motorized, built to execute complex acquisition tasks automatically, scanning large areas or building 3D representations without manual intervention. Axio Imager.Z2 carries the platform's full capability, the level of motorization needed for laser-based or cryogenic microscopy and the most complex workflows.

paragraphs: Research direction shifts. A study that starts with standard widefield fluorescence might later need optical sectioning, or live-cell imaging at controlled temperature, or full confocal laser scanning. Buying a microscope that can't grow into those needs means buying a second one later.

Axio Imager 2 is designed for that growth path directly. Apotome 3 adds structured illumination for optical sectioning down to 180 nm, useful for anything from mitochondrial imaging to dense multi-marker tissue work. An LSM confocal system extends the platform into laser scanning, for deeper optical sectioning and 3D reconstruction. An XL incubator brings elevated-temperature, live-specimen imaging into scope. And because the platform accepts up to 10 filter sets alongside the ZEISS Viluma multi-LED light source family, spectral flexibility scales right alongside the physical expansions.
